care: Phaedra is a tragedy about a queen who falls in love with her stepson, a love she herself knows is wrong. A false accusation follows, and two characters die offstage, reported in speeches. The lesson treats these as the play does, without detail. Berenice, a tragedy in which nobody dies, is a gentler start for young readers.

young.html: Jean Racine was a French playwright who lived at the same time as Molière. Molière wrote comedies that make us laugh; Racine wrote tragedies, serious plays about great people whose strong feelings lead them into trouble.

Racine followed strict rules. The whole story had to happen in one day, in one place, and be about one main problem. No battles on stage, no jumping from country to country. Everything happens in conversations, so every word counts. He wrote in long rhyming lines of twelve syllables.

In Berenice, the Roman emperor Titus loves Queen Berenice, but the Roman people will not accept a foreign queen. Titus must choose between his love and his duty to Rome. He chooses duty, and they part forever. Nobody dies, but everyone's heart is broken. Racine wanted to show that a tragedy can be about sadness, not only about death.

young.name: gb-phaedra
young.cap: Who is who in Racine's two tragedies. Switch between the plays.

young.html: One room, one day. Try writing a tiny play with Racine's rules: two or three characters, one room, and a problem that must be solved before bedtime (who broke the vase? will the family move?). Nothing can be shown except people talking. Act it out. Was it harder to make it exciting with these rules?

full.html: Jean Racine (1639–1699) was orphaned young and educated by the Jansenists of Port-Royal (see Pascal's rungs), who disapproved of the theater. He broke with them to write plays, and between 1664 and 1677 became the leading tragic poet of France. Berenice (1670) and Phaedra (1677) are among his most admired works. After Phaedra he left the public stage, was reconciled with Port-Royal, became the king's official historian, and wrote only two more plays, on biblical subjects, for a girls' school.

French critics of the 1600s, building on their reading of Aristotle's Poetics, asked for the three unities: one action, in one place, within about one day. They also asked for decorum (no violence shown on stage, and noble speech) and verisimilitude (likelihood). Racine wrote in alexandrines, rhymed lines of twelve syllables. These rules suited him: they force everything inward, into what the characters feel and say.

The plot is taken from one sentence of the Roman historian Suetonius: the emperor Titus sent Queen Berenice away from Rome, against his wishes and hers. Titus, newly emperor, must give her up because Rome will not have a foreign queen. Antiochus, who also loves her, has to carry the news. In the end all three part. In his preface Racine argued that a tragedy needs no blood or death; it is enough that the action be great and the feelings tragic.
Racine took the story from Euripides' Hippolytus and the Roman Seneca, and changed it. The setting is Troezen, in Greece. Hippolytus, son of King Theseus, opens the play wanting to leave:

full.text:
My mind is settled, dear Theramenes,
And I can stay no more in lovely Troezen.
In doubt that racks my soul with mortal anguish,
I grow ashamed of such long idleness.
full.author: Jean Racine
full.ed: The Dramatic Works of Jean Racine, George Bell & Sons (Bohn's Library)

full.html: Theseus has been gone for months. Hippolytus secretly loves Aricia, a princess his father has forbidden anyone to marry. Queen Phaedra, Theseus's wife, comes in weak and ill, wasting away from a secret she has told no one:

full.text:
We have gone far enough. Stay, dear Oenone;
Strength fails me, and I needs must rest awhile.
My eyes are dazzled with this glaring light
So long unseen, my trembling knees refuse
Support. Ah me!
full.author: Jean Racine
full.ed: The Dramatic Works of Jean Racine, George Bell & Sons (Bohn's Library)

full.html: Her secret, which her nurse Oenone draws out of her, is that she loves her stepson Hippolytus and hates herself for it. When false news comes that Theseus is dead, the secret slips out. Then Theseus returns alive. Terrified, Phaedra lets Oenone accuse Hippolytus to his father. Theseus banishes his son and calls on the god Neptune to punish him. Phaedra comes to tell the truth, but learns that Hippolytus loves Aricia, and jealousy keeps her silent. Too late, after Hippolytus has been killed, she confesses and dies.

full.name: gb-phaedra
full.cap: The people of Phaedra and how they are bound together. The dashed lines are secrets.

full.html: Passion against reason and duty. Phaedra sees clearly that her love is wrong and fights it, yet cannot master it. Racine's preface says he wanted to show passions as the cause of disorder, so that audiences would hate them. Many readers have also seen in Phaedra the Jansenist idea, learned at Port-Royal, of a person who knows the good and lacks the strength to do it without grace.

Thinking Phaedra is a villain. Racine says she is “neither entirely guilty nor entirely innocent.” The false accusation comes from Oenone's plan, which Phaedra allows out of fear, and she ends by telling the truth.

deep.html: Racine's great rival was the older Pierre Corneille, whose heroes master their passions by will. Racine's characters usually cannot. A rival poet's Phaedra, staged two days after Racine's in 1677, at first drew audiences away from it; time reversed the verdict. Later French writers, Voltaire among them, held up Racine's verse as a model.

Compare Euripides' Hippolytus on this ladder's Greek rung. In Euripides the goddess Aphrodite causes the queen's love and Hippolytus scorns love altogether; Racine gives Hippolytus a love of his own, Aricia, and moves the drama into Phaedra's conscience.

items: Can a person know what is right and still be unable to do it?
Is it right for a ruler to give up personal happiness for the good of the state, as Titus does?
Do strict rules help or hurt an artist?

questions: Titus chooses duty over love. Was he right? What would you have done?
Oenone tries to help Phaedra by lying. Why does that make everything worse?
Why might it be more powerful to hear about an event in a speech than to see it on stage?
Racine followed strict rules about time and place. Do rules ever make you more creative?
Phaedra waits too long to tell the truth. Why is it hard to admit a mistake quickly?
